A specific narrative idea: silhouette figures chase each other through airports, poolsides, lounges and runways. The world of the film is told in cut-paper graphic shorthand, and every scene has a reason to exist
Typography is part of the set. The vertical rules that drop through 'Catch me if you can' double as architecture, bars and elevator cables, and the cast names hang off them like signage
Each scene has its own palette (cyan, saffron/orange, acid green on black, bubblegum pink, midnight blue gradient), and together they read as one deliberate mid-century system
Real texture: hand-cut edges, ink grain, print-like flats, stencilled stars and a glow on the horizon in the last frame
Choreography is clear across the frames: the pursuer and the pursued recur, scale shifts from interiors to a planetary horizon, and the closing frame is a release
Every frame works as a poster; asymmetric, layered compositions with strong figure–ground play
gaps: The type palette is period-correct but conservative. A few names sit as plain labels rather than being integrated as tightly as the title card
The final gradient-and-light-streak frame is more generic than the cut-paper scenes and slightly breaks the material language
Credit placement occasionally lands in leftover space (the Amy Adams frame) rather than being composed into the scene

tells: Custom modular letterforms that break apart into strokes, dots and kana-like fragments. The type is the subject, not a label
High variety across frames: macro letter crop, horizontal scan band, framed grid of glyphs, diagonal dynamic slash, LED dot-matrix, dense collage lock-up 'TOKYO'
Considered neon palette (coral, mint, chartreuse, violet on near-black) with print-misregistration and scanline texture
Frames imply fast, edited choreography: build-up from single glyphs to a saturated final resolve
Layering and density reward pausing; the frames aren't one repeated layout
gaps: The idea ('Tokyo = glitchy neon signage + kana') is a familiar trope; it needs a more specific concept only this piece could own
No image or world beyond type. A, by contrast, builds characters and scenes that carry an emotional arc
Late frames tip toward noise. Clearer hierarchy and moments of restraint would let the final lock-up land harder

tells: A committed single-system aesthetic: everything rendered in ASCII/monospace glyphs on an International Klein-style blue, including a walking figure, a planet, padlocks and coins
Real 3D form is converted to character density (shaded figure, sphere, coin grid), which takes pipeline craft beyond a filter preset
Varied scenes and transitions are implied: character walk, flow field of $ signs, orbiting planet, terminal log, lock cluster, coin array
The terminal text is written for the piece ('Matching Cut Transition("circular")'), a self-aware detail
Against that: the subject is literal (crypto → dollar signs, padlocks, coins), and the monochrome ASCII look is a popular trend
gaps: The idea is literal and obvious: '$', padlocks and coin icons illustrate the brief rather than reframing it. It needs a metaphor viewers would remember
The single blue/white ground flattens hierarchy across frames. Introduce scale shifts, a second value or a moment of break to build an arc like A's palette journey
The terminal-log frame reads as filler text wall. Typographic hierarchy and composition there need the same care as the rendered scenes

tells: One clear idea: a 1960s cat-and-mouse chase told in silhouette, with the credits placed inside the scenes (airport, pool, elevator, piano lounge, night horizon)
The credit lines turn into architecture: the stems of the title letters become the posts of the set, and the green names hang from the elevator cables
Each frame has its own deliberate palette (cyan, orange/yellow, acid green, pink, night blue), so colour does the scene changes
Print texture like a hand-cut stamp (mottled whites, the paper-like woman by the pool) gives it real material instead of vector default
The silhouettes are asymmetric and full of attitude, and the scenes are choreographed as a journey; the small figure in the last frame closes the chase
Scale contrast between the huge title lockup and the small character credits; the 'MUSIC BY' lockup on the piano label is a typographic joke
gaps: It openly draws on Saul Bass / 60s modernism, so it is less original than its execution
The light is mostly flat colour fields; only the last frame uses light as a dramatic tool
The secondary credit type is a fairly standard grotesk, less custom than the title lockup

tells: A kinetic type system built for the subject: Latin and katakana letterforms break apart into modular strokes and dot grids to spell TOKYO
Dense, layered frames: scanlines, dot-matrix fields, offset frames and red bars overlapping, with real texture and grain
The palette (hot pink, mint cyan, acid yellow-green, violet on near-black) is specific and handled with discipline
Strong variety from frame to frame: tight macro letter crop, banded horizontal wipe, framed field of glyphs, diagonal slash, pixel matrix, layered collage. That implies choreographed transitions
The glyph deconstruction is consistent, which shows a designed type system rather than a filter
gaps: The idea is a vibe (glitchy neon Tokyo) more than a story, so it is less memorable than A's narrative conceit
The cyberpunk glitch language is well worn; the piece needs a move that only it could make
There is no human or figurative anchor; the emotional register is all surface energy

tells: A committed single-medium system: everything is built from ASCII/monospace glyphs on an International Klein-style blue, including figures, coins, padlocks and a planet
Real rendering work: glyph density changes to model form and depth (the running figure, the ringed sphere), not just a filter
Varied staging: figure, flowing field, orbiting planet, full-screen code dump, padlocks, and a grid of rotating coins, all linked by match-cut logic (the code even names 'matchcut_engine')
The small reversed-out label boxes ('<<Crypto is...', 'Faster') carry the copy in a voice consistent with the system
gaps: The idea is literal (crypto = code, dollar signs, padlocks, coin icons) and the iconography stays on the obvious surface of the topic
One colour and one texture throughout limits the dynamic range; nothing breaks the system to surprise
The code-dump frame reads as filler text; the copy and type need a stronger editorial voice and scale contrast

tells: A specific narrative idea: a cat-and-mouse chase told through silhouettes, with each frame carrying a different setting (airport lounge, poolside, elevator, cocktail piano, night horizon)
Vertical rules work as the system: they act as architecture, ladders, elevator shafts and descenders, and they cut through the title letterforms, so type and image are one structure
The palette changes with each scene (cyan, saffron/orange, acid green, pink, midnight blue) but the flat-colour system keeps it coherent and in period
Hand-cut, stamped textures on the figures; mid-century screen-print feel; credits are placed inside the scene, not laid on top
The sequence shows choreography: recurring hatted pursuer, location changes and a progression from day to night
Every frame works as a poster
gaps: Benchmark entry; the one gap is that the retro idiom openly leans on 1960s Bass-era precedent, so it scores slightly lower on originality
Light is purely graphic. The final frame's glow hints at depth that the rest of the piece does not develop
A few credit placements (the Steve Eastin/Chris Ellis stack) are more functional than expressive

tells: The letterforms are clearly custom: cut and segmented glyphs mixed with katakana fragments, building toward 'TOKYO'
An unusual neon palette (coral, mint/cyan, chartreuse, violet on near-black) used with discipline
The layouts change a lot between frames: a giant cropped D with a target, a horizontal band with tracked S G, a bordered word-field, a diagonal scatter, dot-matrix glyphs, dense layered collage
Real texture: scanlines, halftone dots, grain and layered transparencies give the frames depth
Assembling and fragmenting the glyphs implies kinetic choreography
gaps: The idea is a familiar 'Tokyo glitch / city-as-signal' trope. It needs a more specific concept that only this piece could have, as C has
Some frames (the dot-matrix one) read as texture without a subject. Each beat should land on a clear image
No human or narrative anchor, and the type rarely carries meaning past the aesthetic

tells: ASCII and character rendering of 3D-ish subjects (a walking figure, a coin, a planet with rings, padlocks, a coin grid) shows real rendering work rather than a preset
Scale and structure change between frames: a character, a flowing particle stream, a planet, a full code screen, a lock triptych, a grid of coins
Match cuts are implied: the code even references 'MatchCut Transition(circular)', and circular forms carry through
Against that: one-colour International Klein-ish blue with white is a well-worn crypto/tech look, and the type is default monospace in highlight boxes ('Crypto is...', 'Faster')
gaps: The idea is literal (crypto = code + coins + locks + '$'). It needs a metaphor a viewer would remember
Typography is default mono slugs. It needs a typographic voice with scale contrast and integration, as in B and C
A single flat blue with no light or material. A second accent or tonal depth would give it hierarchy and atmosphere
